title: Using gravitational potential energy
prior_knowledge_summary: Gravitational potential energy is energy stored by a mass because of its position or height in a gravitational field.
The previous lesson derived ΔE_P = mgΔh from W = Fs for a mass raised steadily in a uniform gravitational field.
Δh is final height minus initial height, and path length does not replace vertical height change.
A negative ΔE_P records a decrease in the gravitational potential energy store.
new_learning: Choose and calculate the correct signed vertical height change in unfamiliar contexts.
Use signed vertical height change to calculate gains and losses of gravitational potential energy.
Rearrange the formula to determine mass, weight or height change.
Separate vertical height change from path length in direct and mixed work-energy problems.

visual_planning.reason: Six distinct planned figures support the route puzzle, controlled definition, derivation, signed changes, reverse solving and final method choice. Assets are deferred in this text-only four-file task.
visual_planning.style: rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch

blocks.title: Two routes, one energy gain
content: A hiker reaches the same balcony by a steep staircase or a long ramp. The ramp route is much longer. Does the hiker gain more gravitational potential energy on the ramp?
Both routes begin and end at the same heights. Near Earth's surface, the energy gain caused by gravity depends on the vertical height change, so both routes give the same gain for the same mass.
The longer route can still involve different work against friction. That is a separate energy transfer.

figure.purpose: Create the need to distinguish path length from vertical height change
figure.brief: A hand-drawn side view of one start point and one balcony reached by a steep staircase and a longer ramp. Mark the same vertical height change for both routes, without equations or numerical answers.
figure.alt_text: A staircase and a longer ramp connect the same lower and upper heights.

blocks.title: Energy stored because of position
blocks.accepted_definition: energy stored by a mass because of its position or height in a gravitational field
content: Gravitational potential energy is energy stored by a mass because of its position or height in a gravitational field.
Raising a book transfers energy into its gravitational potential energy store. Lowering the book transfers energy out of that store.
We normally calculate a change between two heights. The choice of zero level does not affect that change.

figure.purpose: Connect higher position with a larger gravitational energy store
figure.brief: A three-frame teacher sketch of the same book on a floor, desk and shelf. Use one upward height bracket and simple energy-store bars that increase with height.
figure.alt_text: The same book has a larger gravitational potential energy store at greater height.

blocks.title: Carry the previous derivation into calculations
blocks.accepted_definition: product of force and displacement in the direction of the force
content: The previous lesson showed that raising a mass steadily gives F = mg and that W = Fs becomes W = mgΔh.
That work is stored as gravitational potential energy, giving ΔE_P = mgΔh in a uniform gravitational field.

This is a formula to remember: ΔE_P = mgΔh. ΔE_P is the energy change in joules, m is mass in kilograms, g is acceleration of free fall in metres per second squared, and Δh is signed vertical height change in metres.

figure.purpose: Reconnect the previous derivation to the formula used in this lesson
figure.brief: A compact annotated recall ladder beside a slowly lifted box: W = Fs, F = mg, s = Δh, then ΔE_P = mgΔh. Show equal upward lift and downward weight arrows, with a label that this was derived in Lesson 3.
figure.alt_text: The previous lesson's work-done derivation leads to the gravitational potential energy formula used here.

blocks.title: Use the sign of the height change
content: A 2.4 kg toolbox moves from a platform 1.2 m above the floor to a shelf 3.7 m above the floor. Take upward as positive.
The signed height change is Δh = 3.7 - 1.2 = +2.5 m.
ΔE_P = mgΔh = 2.4 × 9.81 × 2.5 = +58.86 J, so the gravitational potential energy increases by 59 J to two significant figures.
If the toolbox returns to the platform, Δh = 1.2 - 3.7 = -2.5 m and ΔE_P = -59 J. The negative sign means the store decreases. It is not an impossible negative amount of energy.
Check: moving upward must give a positive change and reversing the move must give the same magnitude with the opposite sign.

figure.purpose: Teach signed height change and reversal
figure.brief: A two-direction shelf sketch with heights 1.2 m and 3.7 m. Show an upward route labelled Δh = +2.5 m and a downward route labelled Δh = -2.5 m, with no final energy values.
figure.alt_text: Moving between two shelves gives opposite signed height changes for upward and downward travel.

blocks.title: Work backward from an energy change
content: A lift and its load have weight 7.5 × 10³ N. Their gravitational potential energy increases by 4.5 × 10⁴ J. Find the vertical rise.
Because weight mg is already given, use ΔE_P = weight × Δh.
Rearrange before substituting: Δh = ΔE_P/weight = (4.5 × 10⁴)/(7.5 × 10³) = 6.0 m.
The unit check is J/N = (N m)/N = m. The positive energy change also agrees with an upward rise.

figure.purpose: Teach reverse solving with weight supplied directly
figure.brief: A clean calculation map for a lift: known ΔE_P and weight feed into Δh = ΔE_P/weight, followed by a J/N to m unit check. Leave the numerical result space visually separated from the inputs.
figure.alt_text: A reverse calculation uses energy change divided by weight to find vertical rise.

blocks.title: Why the distance travelled feels tempting
content: It feels natural to place the full route length into ΔE_P = mgΔh because work done uses displacement in the force direction. That shortcut fails on a slope because gravity is vertical, not along the slope.
Use the vertical component of the displacement. For a slope of length s at angle θ above the horizontal, Δh = s sin θ.
Path length can still matter when calculating work done by a pulling force or work against resistance. Keep that calculation separate from the gravitational potential energy change.

For an object that starts and finishes at rest, energy conservation gives a useful check: work done by the pull equals the gravitational potential energy gain plus energy transferred to thermal stores by resistance.

figure.purpose: Contrast slope distance with the vertical component used for gravitational potential energy
figure.brief: A right-triangle slope with hypotenuse s, vertical side Δh and angle θ. Add a downward weight arrow and a small crossed-out note showing that s is not Δh.
figure.alt_text: An inclined path has a vertical height change smaller than its slope length.

blocks.title: A reliable gravitational energy routine
content: First choose initial and final positions. Then calculate signed vertical height change as final height minus initial height.
Use ΔE_P = mgΔh, or weight × Δh when weight is given. Rearrange before inserting values, carry units, and round only at the end.
In a mixed problem, calculate work along the force direction and gravitational potential energy from the vertical height change. Use energy conservation to account for any difference.
Finish with a physical check: upward should give a gain, downward should give a loss, and two routes between the same heights should give the same gravitational potential energy change.
Use this near Earth's surface where the gravitational field can be treated as uniform. The point-mass formula for gravitational potential energy belongs to a later topic.
